rationale: A <div> with an onclick handler acting as the Save button. It has no role, so it is announced as plain text rather than as a button; it is not in the tab order, so it cannot be reached by keyboard at all. The primary action of the form is unavailable to anyone not using a mouse.

The same control as a real <button> with visible text. Role, name and keyboard operation all come free from the element. Correctly not selected by the semantics rule — a native control with no overriding role has real semantics — so expected to score as never-looked-at.

A <div> switch whose on/off state exists only as a knob position and an `is-on` class. No role, no accessible name, no aria-checked: the accessibility tree contains no control here and no state. A screen-reader user cannot discover that the setting exists, let alone which way it is set.
The same switch as a <button role="switch"> with aria-checked and an aria-labelledby pointing at its visible label. Role, name and value are all exposed.

The tab strip container: a <div> holding three anchors, styled as a tab bar with one marked current. Nothing carries role="tablist", so the relationship between the strip and the three panels below it exists only visually. Note this element is expected to be never-captured for `semantics` — the div has no role, is not interactive and is not a heading, so the rule does not reach it. That is a coverage finding, not a model error.

The "Loans" tab is an <a href="#panel-…"> presented as a tab. It is announced as a link, so its role contradicts what it looks like and how it behaves, and it exposes no aria-selected, so a screen-reader user cannot tell which of the three is showing. Expected to be never-captured: the semantics rule deliberately skips an <a> that has an href, because a real link with real semantics needs no judgment. Whether that skip is right when the link is dressed as a tab is a question for the expert.

An <a class="btn" href="/reports/lending-summary"> — a link styled as a button. It navigates, so link is arguably the honest role and adding role="button" would be a downgrade that breaks Enter-vs-Space expectations. The counter-reading is that a control which looks like a button sets an expectation about behaviour that its role contradicts. The visual/semantic mismatch is real; whether it rises to a 4.1.2 failure is a judgment call, so the calibrated answer is uncertain rather than a confident pass.

rationale: The control that removes the saved crime fiction search is a <span> with a click handler and nothing else. It has no role, so it is announced as ordinary text rather than as a control; it has no tabindex, so it is not in the tab order and cannot be reached from the keyboard at all. Three of them sit on this page, one per saved search, and as far as the accessibility tree is concerned not one of them exists. The only way to delete a saved search is with a mouse.

rationale: The same control for the crime fiction search, built as a <span role="button" tabindex="0"> with a key handler for Enter and Space. The role is announced, its visible text supplies the name, and it can be operated without a mouse. Note the role is what keeps this element in scope: a native <button> here would have real semantics, the rule would correctly decline to judge it, and the record could never score.
